clue.text: Royal poise and majesty feature together in upbringing

indicators.note: in a down clue an upbringing raises letters from the bottom, so the hidden run is read from below
only the end of the first noun and the start of the second feature, joined together, so the outer letters and the joining word drop away

explanation.surface: A child raised to have the bearing and dignity of royalty.
explanation.walkthrough: In effect a reversed hidden word: 'together' joins poise and majesty, ignoring 'and', and the stretch ISEMAJ that features there is read upwards, as 'in upbringing' asks in a down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: James the First was a king of England and Scotland, so the name is a royal one.

clue.text: A copper putting cuffs on for a little insight

indicators.note: cuffs close round wrists, so the first pieces close round the word for 'for'

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
per means for, as in 'per person'

explanation.surface: A policeman handcuffing someone and gaining a small clue to the crime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'copper' looks like a police officer; it is the metal's symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: An aperçu is a brief glimpse or quick illuminating comment, a small piece of understanding.

clue.text: MPs given big job in secluded house

parts.note: being at home is being in
something secret is hidden away, secluded
Aries is one of the twelve houses of the zodiac in astrology

explanation.surface: Politicians handed a grand post while hiding away in a remote residence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'house' suggests a building, but here it is an astrological house of the zodiac.
explanation.definitionFit: Home Secretaries are MPs appointed to one of the great offices of state, running the UK Home Office.

clue.text: Wounded hero to whom Eros appears mysteriously?

indicators.note: wounded suggests something damaged and out of shape, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A hero struck by Cupid's arrow, the love god having turned up out of nowhere.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of HERO TO WHOM EROS fills both 4 and 20 Down. Eros wounds his victims with love's arrows, so the surface fits the myth.
explanation.definitionFit: Done somehow or other means done in some way nobody can explain, which is to say mysteriously.

clue.text: Puck's happy we agree

parts.note: Puck is also called Robin Goodfellow, so a happy Puck is a jolly Goodfellow; the song 'For he's a jolly good fellow' is followed by the line that agrees

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's mischievous sprite is cheerful, and everyone concurs.
explanation.walkthrough: Puck in A Midsummer Night's Dream is Robin Goodfellow. 'For he's a jolly good fellow', a song sung to toast someone, ends with this chorus of agreement.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is the chorus answering the toast song, everyone present voicing their assent.

clue.text: Fruit harvests constant, this chap making cheese

indicators.note: to harvest is to gather in, so the fruit takes the other pieces inside it

parts.note: a mango is a tropical fruit
c is the usual symbol for a constant, such as the speed of light
he is the pronoun for a man just mentioned

explanation.surface: A farmer brings in fruit steadily and also makes cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: 'harvests' reads as a noun after 'Fruit', but it is a verb meaning gathers in.
explanation.definitionFit: Manchego is a firm Spanish sheep's milk cheese from La Mancha.

clue.text: Only 5% from a pint? Old penny flung in disgust

parts.note: a British pint is twenty fluid ounces, so five per cent of it is one fluid ounce, FL OUNCE
d was the abbreviation for the old pre-decimal penny

explanation.surface: Someone served a tiny measure from a pint throws an old coin down in disgust.
explanation.walkthrough: The imperial pint is 20 fluid ounces, unlike the 16-ounce American pint. Before 1971 British pennies were written d.
explanation.definitionFit: To flounce is to fling oneself about or storm off in a huff, so flounced means went off in a temper.

clue.text: A top play regularly staged to inspire single S American city

indicators.note: to inspire is literally to breathe in, so the single word takes the others inside it

parts.note: a solo is a performance by one person alone

indicators.note: taken in regular stages, so only every other letter of the play words is used

explanation.surface: A first-class play performed often enough to inspire one South American city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'staged' here means in stages, step by step, not performed. The grid spells the city's second word with an O, as the wordplay builds it.
explanation.definitionFit: São Paulo is the largest city in Brazil, and in South America.

clue.text: As good as new in the morning?

parts.note: early means at the start of the day

explanation.surface: Something looks nearly new when you see it at dawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As good as new' looks like one phrase; the definition stops before 'new'.
explanation.definitionFit: Nearly and as good as both mean almost, all but completely.

clue.text: Serving girl's lost one off her trolley

indicators.note: the girl has lost something, so a letter is taken out of the word for her

parts.note: a maid is a female servant
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A waitress has lost a customer who has fallen off her trolley.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off her trolley' is British slang for crazy, not someone toppling from a cart.
explanation.definitionFit: Being off one's trolley is a British idiom for being crazy, mentally unhinged.

clue.text: What a shame one's attending boring day of Latin and English

indicators.note: boring means drilling into, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: diem is the Latin for day, as in carpe diem
an ear is what one attends with when listening

explanation.surface: A sorry state: someone sits through a tedious day of Latin and English lessons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boring' looks like the tedium of the lessons; it means piercing, so EAR goes into DIEM.
explanation.definitionFit: Dearie me is an old-fashioned exclamation of mild dismay, much like saying what a shame.

clue.text: Packs together to fix a bone

indicators.note: to fix is to set something in place, so the single letter is fixed inside the packs

parts.note: in rugby a scrum is where the two packs of forwards bind together

explanation.surface: Pressing pieces together to set a broken bone.
explanation.walkthrough: In rugby the forwards form a 'pack', and the two packs meet in a scrum.
explanation.definitionFit: The sacrum is the triangular bone at the base of the spine.

clue.text: Cliché, irony, etc, the basis for the Budget address?

definitions.meaning: rhetorical devices and expressions such as these

definitions.text: the basis for the Budget address?
definitions.meaning: the UK Budget speech rests on the numbers, the figures, of the speech

explanation.surface: Clichés and irony form the foundation of the Chancellor's Budget speech.
explanation.walkthrough: The Budget is the annual UK government statement of taxes and spending, delivered as a speech by the Chancellor of the Exchequer.
explanation.definitionFit: Cliché and irony are kinds of rhetorical expression; the Budget speech is built on numbers, its figures.

clue.text: Beasts recorded in dwindling numbers

indicators.note: the answer is written down within these words, so its letters run across them

explanation.surface: Animals noted as declining in population.
explanation.walkthrough: The plural of the animal's name can be the same as the singular, so 'Beasts' fits.
explanation.definitionFit: Gnu, another name for wildebeest, can be used as a plural for the African antelopes.

clue.text: Note: 'How did I do on the spelling test, Miss?'

definitions.meaning: the phrase is a warning to take note of what one says

definitions.text: How did I do on the spelling test, Miss?
definitions.meaning: a pupil asking the teacher to assess the written words would say ...?

explanation.surface: A child asks their teacher how they scored on a spelling quiz.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs on into 18 Across. Read as a question, it asks the teacher whether she will grade the words.
explanation.definitionFit: The expression is said to make someone heed a prediction, much as a written 'note' or 'NB' asks attention.

clue.text: I'm not sure I see through plump theatregoer's attire

indicators.note: the hesitation and exclamation are seen through the middle of the word for plump, so they go inside it

parts.note: to plump for is to opt, choose
er is the sound of hesitation or uncertainty
aha is an exclamation of understanding

explanation.surface: An unsure onlooker peers past a stout theatregoer's outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plump' looks like an adjective for the theatregoer; it is the verb, as in 'plump for'.
explanation.definitionFit: An opera hat is a collapsible top hat worn to the theatre or opera.

clue.text: Sort of meal for slicing

indicators.note: slicing means cutting into, so the small word cuts into the rearranged letters
to sort is to rearrange, so these letters are reordered

parts.note: at can mean for, as in apples at a pound each

explanation.surface: A kind of dish meant to be served in slices.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' giving AT is the sense of a price, as in two at a pound. The whole clue also describes the dish.
explanation.definitionFit: A meat loaf is a baked block of minced meat, a dish typically cut into slices to serve.

clue.text: See 15
Circuit of duty in Navy uniform

indicators.note: one piece sits in the other

parts.note: RN is the Royal Navy
Uniform is the NATO alphabet word for U

explanation.surface: A sailor's spell of duty served in Navy uniform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uniform' looks like naval dress; it is the radio code word for the letter U.
explanation.definitionFit: A run can be a regular route or round, like a milk run or a delivery circuit.

clue.text: See 4
Where flight delay may agitate passengers, new plane route urged

definitions.text: Where flight delay may agitate passengers

indicators.note: a new version of the letters means they are put into a fresh order

explanation.surface: Passengers stuck at an airport fume over a fresh route for their plane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' looks like it qualifies the plane route, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The departure lounge is the airport waiting area where passengers sit until boarding, fretting over any delay.

clue.text: Opens up cans to make merry!

indicators.note: making merry suggests getting tipsy and jumbled, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone cracks open some cans of beer to have a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opens up' looks like one phrasal verb; the definition is 'Opens' alone.
explanation.definitionFit: To uncap is to take the cap off a bottle or pen, so uncaps means opens.

clue.text: Anger follows fuel being short — here?

definitions.text: Anger follows fuel being short — here?

indicators.note: follows means the word for anger comes after
something short lacks its end, so the fuel loses its final letter

parts.note: gas is American for petrol, or a fuel itself
rage is fierce anger

explanation.surface: Drivers grow angry when fuel runs out at the filling station.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gas' is the American word for petrol. The whole clue also pictures the place where fuel runs short and tempers flare.
explanation.definitionFit: A garage in Britain can be a filling station, where fuel shortages would make motorists fume.

clue.text: 'Rating scales are infamously low on reliability', heads read

indicators.note: the heads of the words are their first letters, read off in order

explanation.surface: A quoted complaint that ratings scales are notoriously unreliable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rating' looks like a score; in naval use it is a non-commissioned sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Royal Navy a rating is an enlisted seaman, below officer rank.

clue.text: For cruciverbalist women, when life begins?

definitions.meaning: split as ..., the answer is W, the middle of two, and a crossword solver reads W as women
the saying goes that life begins at forty

explanation.surface: A puzzle asks at what age life begins for women who love crosswords.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as TWO'S CORE, the answer gives W, which solvers read as women. The saying 'life begins at forty' gives the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A score is twenty, so two-score is forty, the age when the proverb says life begins.

clue.text: Sort of idiom, initially not a word

indicators.note: initially points to the first letter of the word idiom

parts.note: sh is a call for silence, telling someone not to say a word

explanation.surface: A kind of idiom that, at first, is not really a word at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sort of' looks like it introduces 'idiom'; it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Ish, used on its own in casual speech, means approximately or to some extent.

clue.text: Reason exec at first appears lost at meeting? Gout

definitions.text: Reason exec at first appears lost at meeting?
definitions.meaning: read in two parts, the answer gives an assistant's abbreviation and a word for not on time, which together explain an executive's bewilderment at a meeting
the French goût means taste, a sense of the mouth

explanation.surface: An executive seems confused at a meeting, perhaps because of gout.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as PA LATE, the first part says the personal assistant has not arrived. 'Gout' looks like the joint disease, but it is the French goût, taste.
explanation.definitionFit: The French goût means taste, and the palate is one's sense of taste.

clue.text: Carriage and attendants reading from the same sheet?

parts.note: equi- is the prefix meaning equal or the same
a page is a sheet of a book

explanation.surface: Coach and servants all in agreement, singing from the same hymn sheet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reading from the same sheet' plays on the idiom for being in agreement: an equal page.
explanation.definitionFit: An equipage is a horse-drawn carriage together with its horses and liveried servants.
